legalStatuses.label: Sole proprietorship
legalStatuses.plain: You work in your own name. It is the simplest and cheapest way to start.
legalStatuses.registeredAt: Department of Licensing and Consumer Affairs
legalStatuses.feeNote: The DLCA yearly licence renewal is US$390. A new licence also has a police background check (US$9 a person) and a zoning approval (US$20), and the DLCA quotes the fee for your activity.

legalStatuses.label: Corporation or LLC
legalStatuses.plain: A company is a separate entity from you. It costs more to set up and needs more bookkeeping.
legalStatuses.registeredAt: Office of the Lieutenant Governor, Division of Corporations and Trademarks
legalStatuses.feeNote: A company is registered with the Division of Corporations and Trademarks, then licensed by the DLCA. The Lieutenant Governor's office quotes the filing fees.

launchSteps.label: Choose your business name and check that it is free
launchSteps.plain: Search the name first. A company registers its name with the Division of Corporations and Trademarks.

launchSteps.label: Register the company with the Division of Corporations and Trademarks
launchSteps.plain: Only needed for a corporation or LLC. A sole proprietor does not incorporate.

launchSteps.label: Get your tax identification number
launchSteps.plain: You need an EIN (a federal employer number) or a taxpayer number for the Bureau of Internal Revenue.

launchSteps.label: Apply for your business licence
launchSteps.plain: Every business needs a licence from the Department of Licensing and Consumer Affairs before it starts trading.

launchSteps.label: Register for the gross receipts tax
launchSteps.plain: Every business pays a 5% gross receipts tax once its receipts reach US$225,000 a year. You report it to the Bureau of Internal Revenue.

launchSteps.label: Open a separate bank account for the business
launchSteps.plain: Keeping business money apart from household money makes your numbers clearer and your taxes easier to pay.

launchSteps.label: Register as an employer
launchSteps.plain: With employees you withhold income tax and pay Social Security and Medicare on their wages, and register for territorial unemployment insurance.

incomeTax.label: Income tax (paid to the Virgin Islands)
incomeTax.bracketText: The Virgin Islands copies the US federal tax code: 10% up to US$12,400 of taxable income, 12% up to US$50,400, 22% up to US$105,700, 24% up to US$201,775, 32% up to US$256,225, 35% up to US$640,600, then 37%

contributions.label: Social Security (self-employment tax)
contributions.plain: Self-employed people pay both the employee and employer share: 12.4% on 92.35% of their earnings, up to US$184,500 of earnings a year. Half of it lowers your taxable income.

contributions.label: Medicare (self-employment tax)
contributions.plain: 2.9% on 92.35% of your earnings, with no ceiling. Half of it lowers your taxable income.

calendar.monthlyText: If your receipts are above US$225,000 a year, file and pay the gross receipts tax monthly (Form 720-VI) to the Bureau of Internal Revenue.
calendar.annualTextPersonal: File your income tax return with the Virgin Islands Bureau of Internal Revenue. Below US$225,000 of receipts, file the annual gross receipts return (Form 720-B) by January 30.
calendar.payrollText: With employees: deposit the withheld income tax, Social Security and Medicare, and file the quarterly employer return (Form 941).

notes: The US Virgin Islands has no sales tax. Businesses pay a 5% gross receipts tax on everything they sell once their receipts reach US$225,000 a year, with no deduction for what they buy.

Income tax follows the US federal tax code and rates but is paid to the Virgin Islands Bureau of Internal Revenue, not the IRS (the US federal tax agency). Self-employment tax is on top. Businesses approved by the Economic Development Commission can get large tax reductions: ask the Commission.
A corporation pays the federal rate of 21% plus a 10% territorial surtax (23.1% in total). The owner's own pay is not in the estimate.
